t: Change the Root of a Binary Tree: Rerooting by Climbing Parent Pointers
o: We must make the given leaf the new root while preserving the node set and binary-tree shape rules. The transformation touches only the single path from leaf to root: each node on that path adopts its old parent as its new LEFT child (null at the old root), treats the child we climbed from as its NEW PARENT, and fills its freed right slot with either its displaced left child or whatever legitimate child remains. Example 1 reroots at leaf 7 producing the chain 7 -> 2 -> 5 -> 3, with sideways children (4 stays under 2, 6 moves under 5, 1 becomes 3's right child) shuffled per the two stated rules. Because every Node carries a parent pointer, we can walk upward directly in O(h); the hidden requirement — fixing parent pointers correctly — plus one stale-pointer trap (climbing from a right child must vacate that slot) are what most wrong submissions miss.
k: Only nodes on the leaf-to-root path change; every other subtree hangs untouched beneath its original node.
When climbing from child prev into cur: prev becomes cur's new PARENT, cur's original parent becomes its LEFT child, and cur's right slot takes the old left child whenever that old left is not prev.
The loop must process the OLD ROOT too — its parent slot is null so its left clears — and a climb out of a RIGHT-child position must clear the stale right pointer or the result contains a cycle.

a.n: Approach 1: Iterative Climb Using Parent Pointers
a.i: Start at the leaf holding prev = null (the new root has no parent). At each node cur up to and including the old root: snapshot parent, old left, old right first; then assign new left = parent, new parent = prev; finally choose the new right slot as the old left child unless it is prev, otherwise keep the old right child unless it is prev, otherwise null. Snapshotting before writing makes every case — including climbing from a right child — collapse into three safe assignments.
s: Loop while cur is non-null: save parent = cur.parent, oldLeft = cur.left, oldRight = cur.right.
Set cur.left = parent and cur.parent = prev.
Set cur.right = oldLeft if oldLeft exists and differs from prev; else oldRight if it differs from prev; else null.
Advance prev = cur, cur = parent; return leaf.
a.t: O(h) — one pass over the h nodes of the leaf-to-root path with O(1) work each.
a.sp: O(1) — two traversal pointers regardless of tree size.

a.n: Approach 2: Collect the Path, Then Rewire Downward
a.i: First record the root-to-leaf path with a DFS (handy when parent pointers are absent or untrusted), then walk the recorded list backwards applying exactly the same snapshot-and-reassign rules, taking prev from the next path entry and parent from the previous one. It costs extra memory and a full search, but separates finding the path from transforming it, which many people find easier to reason about and debug.
s: DFS from root collecting every node on the path to leaf into a list.
Iterate i from len(path)-1 down to 0 over nodes cur.
Let prev = path[i+1] if it exists else null, and parent = path[i-1] if i > 0 else null.
Snapshot old children; set cur.left = parent and cur.parent = prev.
Fill cur.right with the old left (if not prev), else the old right (if not prev), else null; return leaf.
a.t: O(n) — the DFS may visit the whole tree once; the rewire pass is O(path length).
a.sp: O(n) worst case for the path list and DFS stack (tree height in the worst case).

w: Use Approach 1 whenever parent pointers are guaranteed (as here): it is O(height), O(1) space, and hard to get wrong once you adopt the snapshot-all-three-fields-first discipline. The classic bugs: skipping the oldLeft-is-prev check (you push your own new-parent chain back down as a child), forgetting parent pointers entirely (passes visual checks, fails this problem's checker), and leaving a stale right pointer when you climbed out of the right slot — that last one creates a cycle the judge reports as Wrong Answer. Edge cases worth testing: leaf whose ancestors all descend through right children, and depth-1 leaves where the old root simply loses its left child. Follow-ups: reroot toward an arbitrary target node instead of a leaf, or perform the same transformation on an N-ary tree.
